title: Weakness upon weakness
hook: his mother carried him in weakness upon weakness, so thank Me and your parents (31:14)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Luqman, and his first advice: put nothing in God's place. Your line was the first advice.

The last weeks of a pregnancy. The back that aches whatever you do. Sleeping propped on pillows, getting up again and again in the night. Then the birth. Then the newborn months, feeding through the night on almost no sleep while the body is still recovering. In the middle of Luqman's advice to his son, the Qur'an interrupts, in God's own voice, to say something about exactly that.

Luqman has just told his son not to ascribe partners to God. Then come two verses that aren't Luqman's; they're God speaking. We have enjoined on the human being concerning his parents. Pickthall: "His mother beareth him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years". Then: give thanks to Me and to your parents; to Me is the journey's end. Weakness upon weakness, wahnan 'ala wahn. Commentators read it as weakness piled on weakness: the strain of pregnancy getting heavier month by month, then birth, then nursing. The verse sees it. Notice the order of thanks: to Me, and to your parents. In one breath, gratitude to God and to the people who carried and raised you are joined. Then the next verse adds a limit. If your parents strive to make you associate with God what you have no knowledge of, don't obey them; and yet keep company with them in this world kindly. Even in disagreement about the most important thing, the kindness stays. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ underlined the mother's place. In a hadith in Bukhari and Muslim, a man asks who most deserves his good company. Your mother, the Prophet says. Then who? Your mother. Then who? Your mother. Then who? Your father. Some commentators connect the threefold mother to three hardships: carrying, birth, nursing. Not every relationship with a mother is easy, and the verse doesn't say it is. What it asks is that people remember what was carried.
screen: `GOD'S VOICE INSIDE LUQMAN'S.` · `WAHNAN 'ALA WAHN.` · `THANK ME, AND YOUR PARENTS.` · `YOUR MOTHER, THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: Think of your mother, or whoever mothered you: a grandmother, an aunt, a foster parent, an older sister, and find one specific thing she carried for you that you probably never thanked her for, a night shift, a school run, a meal she skipped. If she's gone, or things are complicated, you can simply hold her in mind kindly. If you pray, you can pray for her.
Wahn. Weakness, the Qur'an's word for what a mother carries, doubled as wahnan 'ala wahn, weakness upon weakness: pregnancy, birth and nursing, strain piled on strain. Today's word.
Your line: remember what was carried. Kindness stays, even where things are hard. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 534 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WALK MODESTLY, LOWER YOUR VOICE.`

howItsDone: Muslims treat kindness to parents, birr al-walidayn, as a major duty that follows directly after the worship of God, and pray for their parents, living or dead.

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to your mom.
what it means: God's own voice names what a mother carries, and joins thanks to Him with thanks to parents, even when they disagree with you.
what a scholar hears: 31:14–15 is a divine parenthesis inside Luqman's speech; wahnan 'ala wahn; and the threefold mother in Bukhari 5971 and Muslim 2548.
recall: a sign, and a verse of the Qur'an

chat.says: Why does the Qur'an single out mothers when it talks about parents?
options: It names her weakness upon weakness, carrying and nursing, then says thank God and parents.
Because mothers must be obeyed in everything, even in what you believe about God.
Because the verse says only mothers, not fathers, are owed thanks and good company.
chat.meaning: 31:14 says his mother bears him in weakness upon weakness, then: give thanks to Me and to your parents. A hadith names the mother three times.
